stages.name: Observe
stages.instruction: Each dot is a co-located D–T pair (one deuterium + one tritium nucleus) inside a hot plasma. When two like-charged nuclei collide with enough kinetic energy to overcome the Coulomb barrier, they fuse into $^4\mathrm{He} + n$ and release $Q \approx 17.6$ MeV. Sweep the fusion half-life $T_{1/2}^{\mathrm{fus}}$ (a proxy for plasma temperature), toggle LOG, and let the sim run past $T_{1/2}^{\mathrm{fus}}$.
stages.concept: Fusion in a plasma is a stochastic Poisson process: $N(t) = N_0\,e^{-\lambda t}$, with $\lambda = \ln 2 \,/\, T_{1/2}^{\mathrm{fus}}$. Temperature enters through the Gamow factor: $\lambda \propto \exp\!\left(-\alpha/\sqrt{T}\right)$. Hotter plasma $\Rightarrow$ Coulomb barrier tunnelled more often $\Rightarrow$ shorter $T_{1/2}^{\mathrm{fus}}$.

stages.name: Experiment
stages.instruction: A mystery plasma's un-fused $N(t)$ curve (bright orange) is drawn over the plot with three sample points. Tune $T_{1/2}^{\mathrm{fus}}$ until your simulation matches within $\pm 5\%$.
stages.concept: Two plasmas with equal $T_{1/2}^{\mathrm{fus}}$ fuse at the same relative rate, regardless of what temperature or density combination produced it. Matching slopes on a log scale $=$ matching $\lambda$.

stages.name: Evaluate
stages.instruction: No live plasma. A neutron-counter has sampled the reactor at three times $t$ and reported the number of un-fused D–T pairs remaining. Compute $T_{1/2}^{\mathrm{fus}} = \ln 2 \,/\, \lambda$ from the data and type it in. Peek reveals the true depletion curve for $1.5$ s.
stages.concept: From any two readings: $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln(N_1/N_2)}{t_2 - t_1}$, then $T_{1/2}^{\mathrm{fus}} = \ln 2 \,/\, \lambda$. On a log-$N$ plot the slope is $-\lambda$.

labels.tip1: sweep T½ᶠᵘˢ, toggle LOG, let the sim pass T½ᶠᵘˢ
labels.tip2: match the bright orange target — try LOG for a linear fit
labels.tip3: compute λ from two points, then T½ᶠᵘˢ = ln 2 / λ

1.1: T½ᶠᵘˢ is the time it takes for half the D–T pairs to fuse.
1.2: Toggling LOG turns the exponential decay into a straight line — the slope is −λ.
1.3: The dashed teal curve is the theoretical N(t); the solid orange is the stochastic count. They should agree on average — fluctuations reflect the Poisson nature of nuclear collisions.

2.1: The bright orange curve is the target plasma. Match its slope, not just its endpoints.
2.2: On a linear plot, T½ᶠᵘˢ is where the curve crosses N₀/2. On a log plot, matching T½ᶠᵘˢ means parallel lines.
2.3: The Δ% readout in the top-right shows your gap to the target. Under 5% wins.

3.1: Pick any two readings (t₁, N₁) and (t₂, N₂). Then λ = ln(N₁/N₂) / (t₂ − t₁).
3.2: Once you have λ, the fusion half-life is T½ᶠᵘˢ = ln 2 / λ ≈ 0.693 / λ.
3.3: The neutron counter is noisy — the tolerance is ±3%, so small rounding differences are fine. Use peek to see the true depletion curve if you're stuck.
